title: Addition and Subtraction Word Problems: Unknown Starting Number
intro: Sometimes a story tells you the ending, but asks about the beginning. Use the final total and the amount received to find how many there were before. These six stories use small quantities within 20.
html:
“More” does not always mean add the printed numbers

Ella brings 4 library books to her classroom. After she adds them to the shelf, the class has 13 books. Sam sees the words “brings more” and writes 13 + 4. His calculation would be correct for a different question: receiving four more books after already having thirteen. Here, thirteen is the ending total.

Before: an unknown number of books.

Change: 4 books arrive.

After: 13 books.

? + 4 = 13
13 − 4 = 9

There were 9 books on the shelf before Ella arrived.

The four new books are already included in thirteen. Adding them again would count them twice. To find the starting collection, remove the new books from the final collection.

Build the ending first

  1. Put out thirteen counters to represent the books on the shelf now.
  2. Move four counters aside to show the books that just arrived.
  3. Count the nine remaining counters. They represent the books that were there before.
  4. Bring the four counters back. Nine and four return to thirteen.

This check connects subtraction to the story. A child can also count on from four to thirteen to find the missing part, or use the addition fact 9 + 4 = 13. The method can vary while the meaning stays the same.

If the child answers 17: ask, “Could there have been seventeen books before we received more, if there are only thirteen now?” Then label the starting amount with a question mark and put 13 at the end of the story.

Read the time words carefully

Words such as “after,” “before,” and “at first” tell where a quantity belongs. Ask the child to retell the events in order, even when the sentence begins with the ending. A short before/change/after sketch is often enough to make the missing amount clear.

These worksheets focus on receiving an amount and finding the unknown starting collection. They do not mix in stories about losing items or ask for every possible unknown position. The generated quantities stay below twenty, so reading the relationship can receive most of the attention.

Accept an equation that fits

The answer key shows a subtraction equation. An equivalent completed addition equation, such as 9 + 4 = 13, also explains the correct starting amount. Check what the child says the nine represents before requiring a particular written form.
